Just as they were leaving the dining room, the clock tower began to strike midnight. At the final stroke they heard a crash and a sudden piercing cry. A tremendous thunderclap shook the house, and a phrase of otherworldly music drifted through the air. A panel at the top of the stairs sprang open with a loud bang, and Virginia stepped onto the landing, pale as white paper, carrying a little casket. Within a moment they had all rushed up to her. Mrs. Otis seized her in a fierce embrace, the Duke covered her with passionate kisses, and the twins performed a wild war dance around them.

“Good heavens, child! Where have you been?” Mr. Otis said rather angrily, believing she had played some foolish trick on them. “Cecil and I have been riding all over the countryside looking for you, and your mother has been scared to death. You must never play another practical joke like this.”

“Except on the Ghost! Except on the Ghost!” the twins shrieked, leaping about.

“My darling, thank God we've found you. You must never leave my side again,” Mrs. Otis murmured, kissing the trembling child and smoothing her tangled golden hair.

“Papa,” Virginia said quietly, “I've been with the Ghost. He is dead, and you must come and see him. He had been very wicked, but he was truly sorry for everything he'd done. Before he died, he gave me this box of beautiful jewels.”

The entire family stared at her in speechless amazement, but she remained perfectly solemn and serious. Turning, she led them through the opening in the wooden paneling and along a narrow hidden corridor. Washington followed with a burning candle he had snatched from the table. At last they reached a massive oak door studded with rusty nails. Virginia touched it, and it swung open on its heavy hinges. They entered a small, low room with a vaulted ceiling and one tiny barred window. A huge iron ring was fixed into the wall. Chained to it, a gaunt skeleton lay stretched out on the stone floor, apparently reaching with its long, fleshless fingers for an old-fashioned wooden plate and water jug placed just beyond its grasp. The jug must once have held water, for green mold coated its interior. The plate contained only a heap of dust. Virginia knelt beside the skeleton, clasped her small hands, and began to pray silently. The others watched in astonishment as the secret of that terrible tragedy was revealed to them.

Nothing Emma learned afterward required her to revise her poor opinion of Mrs. Elton. Her observations had been fairly accurate. Whenever they met again, Mrs. Elton remained exactly as she had seemed at their second meeting: self-important, presumptuous, overly familiar, ignorant, and ill-mannered. She possessed some beauty and a few accomplishments, but so little judgment that she imagined herself arriving with superior knowledge of the world to brighten and improve a country neighborhood. She considered Miss Hawkins's former position in society so distinguished that only Mrs. Elton's present importance could surpass it.

There was no reason to believe Mr. Elton's opinion differed from his wife's. He appeared proud of her, as well as happy. His manner suggested that he congratulated himself on bringing Highbury a woman whom even Miss Woodhouse could not equal. Most of her new acquaintances were quite satisfied with her, either because they were inclined to praise, unaccustomed to judging, guided by Miss Bates's goodwill, or willing to assume the bride was as intelligent and agreeable as she claimed. Praise of Mrs. Elton thus passed from person to person, as properly it should, without interference from Miss Woodhouse. Emma readily repeated her original contribution, graciously describing her as “very pleasant and very elegantly dressed.”

In one respect Mrs. Elton became even worse than she had first appeared. Her attitude toward Emma changed. Probably offended by the slight encouragement her attempts at intimacy received, she withdrew in her turn, gradually becoming much colder and more distant. Though the result was welcome, the hostility behind it necessarily deepened Emma's dislike. Her behavior toward Harriet, and Mr. Elton's too, was unpleasant: mocking and dismissive. Emma hoped this would quickly cure Harriet's attachment, but the feelings that could inspire such conduct lowered them both greatly in her estimation. Undoubtedly poor Harriet's affection had been sacrificed to frank conversation between husband and wife. Emma's own part in the story had probably also been recounted, in the version least favorable to her and most comforting to him. She was naturally the object of their shared dislike. Whenever conversation ran short, criticizing Miss Woodhouse must always have supplied an easy subject. The hostility they dared not display by openly disrespecting her found freer expression in their contemptuous treatment of Harriet.

Mrs. Elton took a strong liking to Jane Fairfax from the beginning. This was not simply because war with one young woman might make another more attractive; it had been so from the very first. Nor was she content with expressing natural and reasonable admiration. Without invitation, justification, or any right to interfere, she insisted on wanting to help and befriend her. Before Emma had lost her confidence, at about their third meeting, she heard all about Mrs. Elton's chivalrous campaign on Jane's behalf.

Meanwhile, the force of gravity would continually decrease in proportion to the squares of the distances; and so, with my speed increasing enormously, I would eventually reach those remote regions in which the moon's attraction would take precedence over the earth's. Following this reasoning, I judged it unnecessary to burden myself with provisions exceeding what forty days would require.

“There remained, nevertheless, a further difficulty that caused me a degree of uneasiness. It has been noted that balloon ascents to considerable elevations produce, beyond painful respiration, marked discomfort in the head and body. This is often attended by bleeding from the nose and other alarming symptoms, all becoming increasingly troublesome with the height achieved. Such a consideration was somewhat startling. Might these symptoms not intensify without limit, or at least until death put an end to them? I ultimately decided otherwise. Their source must lie in the gradual withdrawal of the ordinary atmospheric pressure from the body's surface, and the resulting swelling of the outer blood vessels, rather than in an actual derangement of the animal system. Difficulty of breathing, by contrast, arises when the atmosphere's density is chemically inadequate for the proper renewal of blood within a ventricle of the heart. Except where this renewal failed, I could therefore perceive no reason why existence might not continue even in a vacuum. The expansion and contraction of the chest, generally termed breathing, is an entirely muscular action, and the cause of respiration rather than its consequence. In brief, I supposed that as the body accustomed itself to the absence of atmospheric pressure, its painful sensations would lessen by degrees; and for bearing them during their continuance, I trusted confidently to the iron toughness of my constitution.

“Thus, with your Excellencies' permission, I have set out some, though certainly not all, of the reflections that brought me to conceive a voyage to the moon. I shall next present the outcome of an enterprise seemingly so daring in conception, and in any case wholly without precedent in the history of mankind.

“On reaching the elevation already specified—three miles and three-quarters—I cast a quantity of feathers out of the car and discovered that my ascent remained sufficiently rapid. There was consequently no need to release any ballast. This pleased me, since I was anxious to keep as much weight aboard as I could bear, for reasons that will become clear later.
